title: 1 Samuel 21:10–15
context: Fleeing Saul, David goes to Achish, king of the Philistine city of Gath, Goliath's hometown. When Achish's servants recognize him as the celebrated warrior of Israel's songs, David, terrified, pretends to be insane. Achish dismisses him as a madman. The headings of Psalms 34 and 56 connect those psalms to this period. WEB’s heading to Psalm 34 is, “By David; when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, who drove him away, and he departed.” Abimelech in that heading is often explained as a royal title for Achish. Psalm 56’s heading places it “when the Philistines seized him in Gath.”

verses.text: David arose and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath.
verses.arminianNotes: David flees "for fear of Saul" to Achish king of Gath. Arminian readers note the desperation of seeking refuge among Israel's enemies, a real and risky choice that shows how low David has fallen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's chosen king seeks shelter in Goliath's own city. The irony underscores how complete David's humbling is, and how dependent he is on God's protection rather than his own plans.

verses.text: The servants of Achish said to him, “Isn’t this David the king of the land? Didn’t they sing to one another about him in dances, saying, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”
verses.arminianNotes: The servants call David "the king of the land" and quote the song from 1 Samuel 18:7. Arminian readers note that David's fame now endangers him, since praise can become a trap when circumstances turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Philistines speak of David as king while Saul still reigns. Even David's enemies unknowingly witness to the kingship God has already appointed for him.

verses.text: David laid up these words in his heart, and was very afraid of Achish the king of Gath.
verses.arminianNotes: David "laid up these words in his heart, and was very afraid." Arminian readers see honest fear in a man of faith. Psalm 56, whose heading places it “when the Philistines seized him in Gath,” models turning such fear into trust in God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Psalm 56’s heading places it “when the Philistines seized him in Gath.” Both traditions see David's fear as real, and the psalm shows how God's grace led him from fear toward trust.

verses.text: He changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands, and scribbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down on his beard.
verses.arminianNotes: David feigns madness, scribbling on gate doors and drooling on his beard. Arminian readers note that this is another act of deception, though many interpreters judge deceiving an enemy who threatened his life differently from deceiving the priest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the ethics of deception in wartime are debated. Whatever one concludes, the scene shows God preserving David through humiliating means, not through strength or status.

verses.text: Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you see the man is insane. Why then have you brought him to me?
verses.arminianNotes: Achish concludes, "the man is insane." Arminian readers note that the ruse works, and David escapes. They also observe that his survival here owes as much to God's mercy as to his own quick thinking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's providence in Achish's dismissal. The heading of Psalm 34 connects that psalm of praise to David's escape when he feigned madness, giving glory for deliverance to the LORD.

verses.text: Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to play the madman in my presence? Should this fellow come into my house?”
verses.arminianNotes: "Do I lack madmen?" Achish refuses to receive him. Arminian readers see David's plan to find refuge in Gath fail, leaving him to seek God's direction elsewhere, a lesson in the limits of human schemes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God closes the door to Gath, keeping his anointed from settling among the Philistines at this time. The closed door turns David back toward Judah, where God's next steps will unfold.
